# Climbing Safety: Moab Area

## Overview
Moab, Utah is one of the premier climbing destinations in North America, offering world-class crack climbing, sport routes, and big wall objectives. The primary areas are Indian Creek, Potash Road (Wall Street), and the cliffs of Castle Valley.

## Potash Road (Wall Street)
Located on Utah Highway 279, less than 5 minutes from downtown Moab. One of the most accessible crags in the area with 441 total climbs:
- 325 trad routes, 99 sport, 17 boulder problems
- Difficulty range: 5.4 TR to 5.12+, with the sweet spot at 5.10–5.11
- Key sectors: Wall Street (150 routes), Long Canyon (146 routes), Day Canyon (55 routes)
- Many moderate classics in the 5.8–5.9 range make this ideal for visiting intermediate climbers

**Critical sandstone rule:** Do not climb during or immediately after rain. Wet sandstone is permanently damaged by climbing — the soft surface tears under friction. Check the forecast; wait at least 24–48 hours after precipitation before climbing sandstone.

## Indian Creek
Located 50 miles south of Moab in Bears Ears National Monument. Indian Creek is the world's premier destination for hand-crack climbing. The parallel sandstone walls produce perfect, consistent cracks from finger to offwidth width.

Characteristics: Routes are typically single-pitch, 60–100 feet, requiring large gear racks (many climbers bring 3–4 sets of cams in the .75"–3" range for a single pitch). Be aware of raptor nesting closures — the Cat Wall and Reservoir Wall have seasonal restrictions posted at the trailhead.

## Rope Systems and Gear
For Moab sandstone trad climbing:
- A 70m dry-treated rope (9.5–10.2mm) is standard
- Large rack: doubles or triples in hand-to-fist sizes (.75"–3") are often needed
- Wear a helmet — rockfall is a constant hazard, especially on popular routes with traffic above

## Belay and Anchor Safety
- Use a locking carabiner on your belay device, clipped to the belay loop only
- Build anchors using SERENE-A: Solid, Efficient, Redundant, Equalized, No Extension, Angle under 60°
- Assisted-braking devices (Grigri) are popular but do not eliminate the need for an active brake hand

## Communication and Emergency
Moab has spotty cell coverage. File a trip plan with a trusted person. The nearest hospital with trauma capability is Moab Regional Hospital (719 W 400 N, Moab). For emergencies in the backcountry: 911 may not connect — a satellite communicator (Garmin inReach, SPOT) is strongly recommended for remote crags.

## Seasonal Conditions
- **Spring (March–May)** and **Fall (Sept–Nov)**: Best seasons. Mild temps, stable weather.
- **Summer**: Extreme heat. Early morning starts only; off the wall by noon.
- **Winter**: Cold but often climbable on south-facing walls. Watch for ice on approaches.

# Gear Guide: Desert and Slickrock Conditions

## Clothing for the Colorado Plateau
Desert conditions demand very different gear choices than alpine environments. Heat, UV, wind, and dramatic day-to-night temperature swings (often 40°F+) are the primary factors.

**Sun protection is the top priority:**
- Long-sleeve sun shirts (UPF 50+) are more effective than sunscreen alone and don't wash off with sweat
- Wide-brim hat (3"+ brim) to protect face, ears, and neck — critical for long days on exposed slickrock
- Lightweight gaiters prevent sand and debris from entering shoes on sandy trail approaches

**Layering for desert:**
- Base: Lightweight merino wool or synthetic moisture-wicking shirt. Merino is preferred — it manages odor over multi-day trips and feels comfortable even when damp from sweat.
- Mid: A lightweight puffy or fleece for evenings and early mornings. Desert nights drop rapidly after sunset.
- Shell: A wind/rain layer. Summer monsoons arrive fast with little warning; a packable hardshell (GORE-TEX or similar) weighs little and can prevent hypothermia from a soaking rainstorm at elevation.

## Footwear
- **Trail runners** are the preferred footwear for most Moab hiking — they drain quickly, dry fast, and the low profile helps with friction on slickrock
- **Sticky rubber soles** (Vibram Megagrip, La Sportiva FriXion) are critical for sandstone — look for this spec when buying desert hiking shoes
- **Approach shoes** are ideal for routes that mix hiking and scrambling (common in Canyonlands and on routes to climbing crags)
- Avoid smooth-soled boots — sandstone is treacherous when sandy or wet regardless of sole type

## Pack Weight
For day hiking in Moab:
- Water (4 liters = 8.8 lbs in summer) is the heaviest item — plan accordingly
- Keep total pack weight under 20 lbs for a day hike; lighter is better in heat
- A 20–30L daypack is appropriate; larger packs trap heat against your back

## Key Materials
- **GORE-TEX**: Waterproof/breathable shell fabric — useful for monsoon season (July–September)
- **Dyneema/DCF**: Ultralight shelter and pack material; useful for lightweight desert backpacking
- **Merino wool**: Ideal base and mid-layer material; handles temperature swings well and resists odor on multi-day trips

## Navigation Gear
- Physical topo map (Nat Geo Trails Illustrated maps for Arches #211 and Canyonlands #226 are the standard)
- Compass
- GPS device or phone with Gaia GPS downloaded offline
- Satellite communicator (Garmin inReach Mini recommended) for backcountry trips away from cell coverage

## Climbing-Specific Gear for Moab
For sandstone crack climbing at Indian Creek or Potash Road:
- Crack gloves (Black Diamond or Trango) to protect hands on repeated hand-jam pitches
- Large cam rack: 3–4 pieces each in .75", 1", 1.5", 2", 3" sizes (Black Diamond Camalots recommended)
- 70m dry-treated rope (9.5–10mm)
- Helmet — mandatory for both leader and belayer

# Hiking Essentials: Arches & Canyonlands

## Overview
Arches and Canyonlands National Parks near Moab, Utah offer some of the most spectacular hiking in the American Southwest — and some of the most unforgiving conditions. Park rangers respond to hundreds of search and rescue incidents annually, primarily due to heat exhaustion, dehydration, and getting lost.

## Arches National Park Trails
Most trails are easy to moderate and use cairn markers across rock surfaces. Highlights:
- **Delicate Arch** (3 mi round-trip, strenuous) — the iconic hike; significant sun exposure with no shade
- **Devil's Garden Loop** (7.8 mi, strenuous) — fins, fins fins, and 8 arches including Landscape Arch
- **Landscape Arch** (1.6 mi, easy) — world's longest natural arch; continuing past this point becomes strenuous

Rules: Do not walk on biological soil crusts (dark, bumpy ground between rocks). Do not enter or stand in ephemeral pools (sandstone basins). Climbing on or rappelling off any arch is strictly prohibited.

## Canyonlands National Park Trails

**Island in the Sky:**
- Easy: Mesa Arch (0.6 mi, classic sunrise), Grand View Point (1.8 mi)
- Moderate: Upheaval Dome (0.6 mi), Aztec Butte (1.4 mi), Neck Spring (5.6 mi)
- Strenuous: Gooseberry Canyon (4.6 mi, steepest in park), Syncline Loop (8.1 mi — most park rescues happen here), Murphy Loop (10.8 mi)

**The Needles:**
- Easy/Moderate: Pothole Point (0.6 mi), Cave Spring (0.6 mi), Slickrock (2.4 mi)
- Strenuous: Druid Arch (10.8 mi, one of the most spectacular views in the park), Confluence Overlook (11 mi), Salt Creek Canyon (22.5 mi multi-day)

**The Maze:** Reserved for serious backcountry — trails are steep, unmarked, and require topo maps and high-clearance 4WD access.

## The Ten Essentials for Desert Hiking
1. Navigation — topo map + compass; cell service is spotty throughout both parks
2. Sun protection — SPF 50+, UV-rated sunglasses, wide-brim hat; UV is intense at 4,000–6,000 ft elevation
3. Insulation — temperature swings of 40°F between day and night are common
4. Illumination — headlamp; afternoon starts frequently end after dark
5. First-aid supplies — moleskin, ace bandage, electrolyte tablets
6. Fire — lighter and matches; desert conditions are extremely dry
7. Repair tools and knife
8. Nutrition — 1 extra day of food minimum
9. Hydration — carry 2–3 liters for front-country, 4+ liters for backcountry
10. Emergency shelter — space blanket at minimum

## Navigation
Download offline maps before you lose cell service. Always share your intended route and return time with someone not on the trip. Cairns mark routes across slickrock — do not build unauthorized cairns.

# Leave No Trace: Canyon Country and Moab Region

## Why LNT Matters More in the Desert
Desert ecosystems are extraordinarily fragile and slow to recover. Biological soil crust — the dark, bumpy, sometimes black or gray ground between rocks — is a living community of cyanobacteria, lichens, and mosses that took decades to form. A single footstep can destroy what took 50–250 years to grow. This crust is critical: it stabilizes soil against wind erosion, fixes nitrogen, and retains moisture.

**The most important LNT rule in canyon country: walk on rock, sand, or established trail. Never step on biological soil crust.**

## The 7 LNT Principles Applied to Moab

**1. Plan Ahead and Prepare**
Check current fire restrictions (common in summer), flash flood forecasts, and trail conditions before departing. Permits are required for some backcountry areas in Canyonlands (The Maze, Salt Creek Canyon). Download offline maps — cell service is unreliable throughout the canyon country around Moab.

**2. Travel and Camp on Durable Surfaces**
Stick to established trails and designated campsites. In Arches, stay on trail, rock, or sandy washes. In Canyonlands backcountry, camp on slickrock or sandy sites at least 200 feet from water sources, archaeological sites, and other campers. The Needles and Island in the Sky have designated backcountry sites — camp only there.

**3. Dispose of Waste Properly**
Human waste: In canyon country, catholes (6–8 inches deep, 200 feet from water, trails, and camp) are the minimum. In many high-use desert areas and slot canyons, pack-out systems (WAG bags, Restop) are required or strongly recommended — solid waste doesn't decompose in dry desert conditions. Pack out all toilet paper. Pack out all food waste — nothing decomposes quickly in the desert.

**4. Leave What You Find**
Arches and Canyonlands contain irreplaceable archaeological resources: petroglyphs, pictographs, granaries, and middens. It is illegal to touch, mark, or collect any archaeological artifact. Oils from skin degrade rock art. Look with your eyes, not your hands.

**5. Minimize Campfire Impacts**
Campfires are prohibited in most of Canyonlands backcountry and discouraged throughout. Use a camp stove. Where fires are permitted, use a fire pan (required in some areas), keep fires small, burn only wood to ash, and carry out all ash. Fire danger is extreme in summer — check current restrictions every time.

**6. Respect Wildlife**
Maintain 150 feet from large mammals. Never feed wildlife — this causes habituation and often leads to the animal's destruction. Store food in hard-sided bear canisters or hang food in bear country. Ravens are extremely clever and will raid unattended packs; never leave food unattended.

**7. Be Considerate of Other Visitors**
Moab trails receive heavy visitation. Yield to uphill hikers. Keep voices low; sound carries far in canyon country. Leave drones at home — they are prohibited in all National Parks.

# Nutrition and Hydration: Desert Conditions

## Water: The Critical Factor in Moab
Dehydration is the leading cause of search and rescue callouts in Arches and Canyonlands. In summer heat (100°F+), the body loses 1–1.5 liters of water per hour during moderate hiking. Most people severely underestimate their water needs.

**Minimum water requirements:**
- Front-country day hikes: 2–3 liters per person
- Backcountry day hikes (summer): 4+ liters per person
- Backpacking: 4–6 liters per day in summer, 2–3 liters per day in cooler seasons

Start hydrating the evening before a big day. Urine should be pale yellow — dark yellow or amber means you're already dehydrated.

**Water sources in canyon country** are scarce. Reliable sources: developed campground spigots, visitor center fill stations. Backcountry sources: seasonal springs, potholes (treat all backcountry water before drinking). Many trails in Arches and Canyonlands have zero water sources — carry everything you need from the trailhead.

## Electrolytes
Drinking large amounts of plain water without electrolyte replacement causes hyponatremia (dangerously low sodium). Signs: headache, nausea, confusion, muscle cramps — easily mistaken for dehydration. Treatment: electrolyte replacement, not more plain water.

In summer desert conditions, supplement with electrolytes every 1–2 hours: Nuun tablets, Liquid IV, Precision Hydration packets, or simply salty snacks (pretzels, crackers, salted nuts). Target 300–500mg sodium per hour during heavy exertion in heat.

## Calorie Needs
Desert hiking burns calories at an elevated rate due to heat stress and uneven terrain (slickrock requires constant micro-adjustments):
- Moderate day hiking: 400–500 extra calories per hour
- Technical scrambling or climbing: 600–800 cal/hour

**Best desert-ready foods:**
- Nuts and nut butter: 160–200 cal/oz, no refrigeration, heat stable
- Jerky and meat sticks: high protein, sodium replaces electrolytes
- Dates and dried fruit: fast carbs, concentrated calories
- Dark chocolate: holds up to heat better than milk chocolate; 150 cal/oz
- Tortillas over bread: don't crush, lower moisture content

Avoid foods that melt, spoil, or require cooking in extreme heat unless you have a good insulated container.

## Timing and Heat
Eat before you're hungry; drink before you're thirsty. In heat, appetite suppression is common even when caloric need is high. Schedule snack breaks every 60–90 minutes regardless of hunger. Eat larger meals during cooler morning and evening hours when digestion is more comfortable.

## Monsoon Season (July–September)
Summer monsoons bring dramatic afternoon thunderstorms. Humidity spikes during monsoon season, increasing sweat rate even when temperatures moderate slightly. Increase water and electrolyte intake during monsoon months. Be aware that heavy monsoon rain rapidly raises flash flood risk in canyon drainages.

# Personal Hike Log — Trails I Have Done

This is a personal hiking journal. These are trails the user has personally hiked and completed firsthand in and around Moab, Utah. Hikes done: Slickrock, Corona Arch, Delicate Arch, Wild Horse Slot Canyon.

---

## Slickrock Trail
- **Location:** Moab, Utah (Sand Flats Recreation Area)
- **Difficulty:** Easy
- **Best For:** Getting a feel for slickrock terrain, mountain biking crossover trail
- **Personal Notes:** A fun, accessible trail on the famous sandstone slickrock surface that Moab is known for. Great introduction to desert hiking on exposed rock.
- **Tips:** Wear grippy shoes — the sandstone traction is surprisingly good but smooth-soled shoes are slippery. Bring more water than you think you need.
- **Season:** Year-round; avoid midday in summer heat.

---

## Corona Arch
- **Location:** Near Moab, Utah (off Hwy 279 along the Colorado River)
- **Difficulty:** Moderate
- **Distance:** ~3 miles out and back
- **Best Part:** Climbing up right next to the arch — the scale of it is incredible up close. Larger than the famous Delicate Arch.
- **Tips:** Watch for trains — the trail crosses active railroad tracks near the trailhead, so look both ways. The route involves a couple of short ladder/rope-assist sections on slickrock.
- **Season:** Spring and summer. Go early in summer to beat heat. Spring is ideal.
- **Personal Notes:** The arch itself is massive and you can walk right under and around it. Less crowded than Delicate Arch.

---

## Delicate Arch
- **Location:** Arches National Park, Moab, Utah
- **Difficulty:** Moderate
- **Distance:** ~3 miles out and back
- **Best Part:** The arch itself — the reveal at the top of the trail where it suddenly comes into view is one of the most iconic moments in all of Utah hiking.
- **Tips:** Take your time on the steep sections of the trail — there are exposed ledges near the top that require careful footing. No shade on the upper trail. Start early.
- **Season:** Spring and summer. Sunrise and sunset hikes are especially rewarding — the arch glows red in late afternoon light.
- **Personal Notes:** Worth every step. The crowds are manageable if you go early morning. The final bowl approach to the arch is unlike anything else.

---

## Wild Horse Slot Canyon
- **Location:** San Rafael Swell area, Utah (southeast of Price, northwest of Moab)
- **Difficulty:** Moderate
- **Best Part:** The entire canyon — the narrow walls, light beams, and sculpted sandstone make it a full sensory experience from start to finish.
- **Tips:** **Watch the weather forecast carefully — flash floods are extremely dangerous in slot canyons.** Never enter if there is rain in the forecast anywhere in the watershed, even miles away. Check weather for the entire region, not just the trailhead.
- **Season:** Spring and summer. Avoid monsoon season (July–September) due to flash flood risk.
- **Personal Notes:** One of the most beautiful slot canyons in the region. The colors and texture of the walls are incredible. A must-do if you can go on a clear weather day.

# Desert Survival: Colorado Plateau and Moab Region

## The Rule of Threes in Desert Context
In canyon country, the order of priorities shifts slightly from general wilderness survival:
- **3 minutes** without air or in flash flood water
- **3 hours** without shade in extreme desert heat (temperatures exceed 100°F July–August in Moab)
- **3 days** without water — but in summer desert heat, severe dehydration can incapacitate in hours
- **3 weeks** without food

**Heat is the primary killer.** Most search and rescue incidents in Arches and Canyonlands involve heat exhaustion or dehydration, not injury.

## Heat Survival
Avoid hiking between 10 AM and 4 PM in summer. Seek shade — canyon walls, overhangs, and rock fins provide relief. Signs of heat exhaustion: dizziness, weakness, nausea, cessation of sweating. Move to shade immediately, elevate legs, and hydrate slowly with water and electrolytes. Heat stroke (confusion, loss of consciousness, hot dry skin) is a medical emergency — cool the victim rapidly and activate emergency services.

Flash floods occur suddenly, even in clear skies, when rain falls miles away in the watershed. Never camp in a wash. If water begins rising or you hear a roaring sound upstream, immediately move to high ground — do not try to outrun moving water.

## Water in the Desert
Water sources in canyon country are scarce and often unreliable. Cryptobiotic seeps and potholes may be the only sources for miles. Do not contaminate potholes — they support entire micro-ecosystems and may be the only water source for wildlife in the area.

Purification: all backcountry water must be treated. Boiling (1 minute), a hollow-fiber filter (Sawyer, Katadyn), or chemical tablets (Aquatabs) are all acceptable. UV purification (SteriPen) works but requires batteries and clear water.

Carry 4+ liters per person for any backcountry day in summer.

## Navigation and Getting Found
Cell service is unreliable in most of the canyon country around Moab. Before any backcountry trip:
- Download offline topo maps (Gaia GPS, CalTopo, or the NPS app)
- Carry a physical topo map and compass
- File a trip plan with someone who will call for help if you don't return
- Consider a satellite communicator (Garmin inReach) for remote trips

If lost: stay put. Searchers will converge on your last known location. Use a signal mirror in open canyon country — visible for miles. Three whistle blasts is the universal distress signal.

## Flash Flood Protocol
- Monitor weather not just overhead but across the entire watershed upstream
- "Turn around, don't drown" — 6 inches of moving water can knock a person down; 12 inches can sweep a vehicle
- If caught in a slot canyon during a flood, climb the walls as high as possible and hold on
- Never camp in washes, drainages, or canyon floors without checking the forecast
